reason: The sources contain 12 distinct, highly surprising claims about SN 1181 and its remnant that are supported by at least two independent sites.
story: In 1181, astronomers witnessed a rare cosmic blast: supernova SN 1181. Normally, a supernova obliterates the star. But in this case, something survived. At the center of the remnant IRAS 00500+6713 lies WD J005311, a zombie white dwarf. This star is the surviving product of a double degenerate merger where a carbon-oxygen white dwarf crashed into an oxygen-neon white dwarf. This collision triggered a sub-luminous Type Iax supernova. X-ray data from the XMM-Newton telescope revealed that the surviving central star is currently blowing an intense stellar wind enriched with carbon-burning ashes. This fast stellar wind crashes directly into the slow supernova ejecta, creating a highly complex and chaotic interaction zone. This unique stellar survivor shows that some stars can live through their own explosions.
angle: A zombie star survived its own supernova explosion when two white dwarfs merged, and it continues to blow an intense wind of carbon-burning ashes into space.

claims.claim: SN 1181 was a supernova first observed in the year 1181.
IRAS 00500+6713 is the remnant of the supernova SN 1181.
The supernova SN 1181 and its remnant IRAS 00500+6713 are associated with a rare Type Iax supernova.
The central star of the IRAS 00500+6713 remnant is designated as WD J005311.
WD J005311 is a white dwarf star.
WD J005311 is the surviving product of a merger of two white dwarfs.
The merger that produced the central star involved a carbon-oxygen white dwarf and an oxygen-neon white dwarf.
The central star WD J005311 produces an intense stellar wind.
The stellar wind of the central star is enriched with carbon-burning ashes.
The IRAS 00500+6713 system has been observed and analyzed using X-ray data from the XMM-Newton telescope.
The remnant features an interaction between the supernova ejecta and the stellar wind of the central star.
IRAS 00500+6713 is catalogued as an infrared source.

disputed: The historical association of SN 1181 with the supernova remnant 3C 58 and its pulsar is now disproved because 3C 58 is much older (3500 to 5000+ years old); the script should leave this out to avoid confusion.
The central star is occasionally designated as WS35 in optical studies; the script should stick to its primary designation WD J005311.
A recent study estimates the exact explosion year as 1152 plus or minus some decades, but since this is consistent with 1181, the script should stick to the historically recorded date of 1181.
